q: Why do singers need to give consonants as much attention as vowels?
correct: Consonants carry the text of the song and make it intelligible
distractors: Consonants supply most of the resonance and tonal color of the voice
Consonants are louder than vowels and must be balanced against them
Consonants set the pitch that vowels must then match
explain: The chapter calls consonants an integral part of communicating the message of song, so they are essential for understanding the text.

q: What is "vowel pollution"?
correct: Vowels preceding or following a consonant are compromised because the consonant was formed inefficiently
distractors: Extra vowel sounds are added at the end of every sung word because the singer releases the consonant too slowly and too late
Vowels are sung too loudly and cover the consonants that come before and after them
Vowels become nasal because the soft palate stays lowered during the neighboring consonants
explain: The book uses the term for singers compromising the preceding and subsequent vowels when they do not form consonants efficiently.

q: Which of these is one of the primary articulators for consonants?
correct: The alveolar ridge behind the top front teeth
distractors: The false vocal folds
The diaphragm
The lower ribs
explain: The primary articulators are the lips, teeth, tongue, alveolar ridge, hard palate, and soft palate, plus proper jaw position.

q: What does efficient articulation of a consonant mean?
correct: Using only the articulators needed to form the consonant and nothing more
distractors: Exaggerating every articulator so the consonant is heard in a large hall
Holding the consonant as long as the vowel that follows it
Keeping the jaw completely still while forming every consonant
explain: Singers should use only the articulators necessary to form a consonant; otherwise neighboring vowels are compromised.

q: What happens when the initial consonant of a word is formed too slowly?
correct: The pitch may be flat, and the singer scoops up to the pitch on the vowel
distractors: The pitch may be sharp, and the singer slides down to the pitch on the vowel
The vowel is shortened so that the word ends well before the next beat arrives
The consonant becomes voiced even if it is written as an unvoiced consonant
explain: A slow initial consonant delays arrival at the intended pitch, so the singer scoops up to it on the subsequent vowel.

q: Why are [w] and "y" ([j]) treated as vowels when singing?
correct: They are glides, formed like [u] and [i] and moved quickly into the next vowel
distractors: They are formed with the soft palate lowered, like nasal consonants, and carry pitch
They are unvoiced sounds produced with breath moving through the open glottis
They are formed by sealing the tongue against the roof of the mouth, like plosives
explain: The book says [w] and y are technically glides: [w] is like [u] and [j] like [i], moving quickly to the following vowel.

q: What distinguishes an unvoiced consonant from a voiced one?
correct: Unvoiced consonants involve no vocal fold vibration and are shaped by breath through the open glottis
distractors: Unvoiced consonants are formed only with the lips and teeth, while voiced consonants use only the tongue and soft palate
Unvoiced consonants require the soft palate to be lowered so that breath can escape through the nose and mouth
Unvoiced consonants carry the pitch of the phrase, while voiced consonants are only noise
explain: Unvoiced consonants have no vocal fold vibration, whereas voiced consonants carry pitch.

q: Which group consists entirely of voiced consonants?
explain: [b], [d], [g], [v], and [z] are voiced; [p], [t], [k], [f], and [s] are their unvoiced partners.

q: Which group consists entirely of unvoiced consonants?
explain: [p], [t], [k], [f], and [s] are produced without vocal fold vibration; [b], [g], and [v] are voiced.

q: What can happen if the final "t" in "mist" is not pronounced?
correct: The word sounds like "miss" and the meaning may be misunderstood
distractors: The word sounds like "missed" and the tense changes
The preceding vowel becomes a diphthong
The pitch of the phrase rises out of tune
explain: Final consonants are easily overlooked, and without them a word can be confused with another word or not understood at all.

q: When singing "blow" too slowly, what unintended result can occur?
correct: An extra vowel such as a schwa appears, making it sound like "buh-lo"
distractors: The [l] is dropped so that the word sounds like "bow" and the vowel is shortened
The [b] becomes unvoiced, so the word sounds like "plow" instead of "blow"
The vowel [o] becomes a glide beginning with [w], so the word sounds like "bwo"
explain: Consonant clusters need two distinct movements, and singing them too slowly inserts an unintended vowel between them.

q: For which consonants does the book describe the jaw lowering phase as the most significant source of pitch difficulty?
correct: [j], [s], [v], and [z], where the jaw closes to some extent
distractors: [g], [k], and [ŋ], where the tongue seals the roof of the mouth
[l], [t], and [d], where the tongue tip touches the ridge
[m], [n], and [ŋ], where the soft palate is lowered
explain: For [j], [s], [v], and [z] the jaw closes, and as it lowers again the first formant rises, raising perceived pitch.

q: Why does singing [g] too slowly in "God" create a problem?
correct: The jaw lowers too slowly from the closed position to [ɑ], so a diphthong occurs
distractors: The tongue tip curls back toward the palate, creating a retroflex sound before the vowel begins
The soft palate lowers and the vowel becomes nasal, so the word sounds like "gnod"
The [g] becomes unvoiced and the word sounds like "cod" because the folds stop vibrating
explain: The mouth is relatively closed for [g], and if the jaw drops too slowly for the vowel [ɑ], a diphthong results.

q: What does R. Miller recommend for how classical singers should execute [l]?
correct: A flick of the tongue with a quick return to rest against the lower teeth
distractors: A firm press of the whole tongue blade against the hard palate
Sustaining it as long as possible to keep the line legato
Placing the tongue tip well behind the front teeth on the roof of the mouth
explain: Miller says a flick and quick return prevents [l] from becoming a lazy, liquid consonant that encourages transitional sounds.

q: How is the glide [w] (as in "wonder") formed, according to the book?
correct: Sing [u] with slightly more lip pucker and move quickly to the next vowel
distractors: Sing [i] with the tongue close to the hard palate and move quickly on to the vowel
Close the lips completely and release them with a burst of air into the next vowel
Place the tongue tip on the alveolar ridge and flip it once before the next vowel
explain: [w] is formed like [u] with a bit more pucker; it emerges in the quick transition to the following vowel.

q: Why might a singer use an unvoiced consonant when entering on a high pitch?
correct: The breath is already moving when the pitch begins, easing coordination of glottal closure and airflow
distractors: Unvoiced consonants raise the first formant and make the pitch easier to reach
Unvoiced consonants keep the vocal folds firmly closed before the vowel
Unvoiced consonants allow the singer to skip the inhalation before the phrase
explain: Coordinating closure and airflow on a high pitch is complicated; starting airflow on the unvoiced version means breath is moving when pitch begins.

q: When singing with a microphone, why should singers be mindful of unvoiced plosive consonants?
correct: They can cause pops or distortion if sung too close or with unamplified breath pressure
distractors: They disappear from the amplified sound and make the words unintelligible to the audience and the sound engineer
They force the singer to add a neutral syllable after each word to release the pressure
They make the sound flat by lowering the first formant and reducing the vocal fold closure
explain: Plosives can pop when sung close to the mic or with the same breath pressure used without amplification.

q: How is a flipped "r" described in the book?
correct: Like "vedy" for "very": one quick, light contact of the tongue on the alveolar ridge
distractors: A tongue flutter on the ridge, sustained by fairly high breath pressure and a relaxed tongue tip
The tongue tip curled back toward the palate while the jaw stays closed for the whole word
The back of the tongue placed against or near the uvula, producing a rolled guttural sound
explain: The flipped "r" touches the alveolar ridge more quickly and with less firm contact than "d," and makes only one contact.

q: What does the ending retroflex (American) "r" do, and how should classical singers treat it?
correct: It dramatically lowers the third formant, so classical singers should avoid it
distractors: It dramatically raises the first formant, so classical singers should double it
It lowers the second formant, so classical singers should extend it
It has no acoustic effect and is acceptable in every style
explain: The tongue tip curling back creates a large cavity and lowers F3; it is avoided in classical music but suits contemporary styles.

q: According to the rules given for singing Italian, how should "r" be formed between two vowels?
correct: Flipped
distractors: Rolled
Retroflex
Guttural
explain: The Italian rules are to flip an "r" between two vowels, roll it next to a consonant, roll a final "r," and never use a retroflex "r."

q: According to Richard Miller, which consonants should be anticipated slightly ahead of the beat in classical singing?
correct: Unvoiced consonants, since they carry no pitch
distractors: Voiced consonants, since they carry pitch
Only the nasal consonants [m], [n], and [ŋ]
Only consonants at the ends of phrases
explain: Unvoiced consonants can precede the beat while voiced ones belong on the beat because they carry pitch, letting the vowel land on the beat.

q: In contemporary styles, what effect does placing consonants ahead of the beat typically create?
correct: A sense of tension or aggressiveness
distractors: A more relaxed, laid-back feeling
A smoother legato with less articulation
A darker vowel color and lower first formant
explain: Consonants ahead of the beat add tension or aggressiveness, while behind the beat they create a more relaxed feel.

q: What is the goal of the "Hang-gun-num-ee" exercise?
correct: Sustaining the nasal consonants [ŋ], [n], and [m] on one pitch while keeping the jaw lowered
distractors: Practicing quick release of the unvoiced plosives [p], [t], and [k] while keeping the jaw closed and firm
Learning to roll the "r" with high breath pressure and a relaxed tongue on every syllable of the phrase
Practicing the flipped "r" between two vowels while the soft palate is fully lowered
explain: The exercise moves quickly through vowels to sustain each nasal consonant, starting with "hang" to lower the jaw and keeping it lowered.

q: What is the purpose of snapping the fingers in the exercise for final consonants?
correct: It shows whether a singer perceives the timing of the release accurately
distractors: It keeps the singer on the beat throughout the whole phrase and the whole song
It trains the tongue to return to its resting position after each final consonant
It reminds the singer to inhale quickly before the final consonant is released
explain: Snapping at the moment of release reveals immediately if a singer does not perceive the release precisely; repeat until correct.

q: Why can lack of attention to a final voiced consonant such as [m] cause flat pitch?
correct: Singers may relax breath support too soon on the voiced final consonant
distractors: The soft palate rises too high and cuts off the resonance of the final consonant
The tongue curls back and lowers the third formant during the final consonant
The consonant is anticipated before the beat, so the vowel is late and the pitch drifts
explain: Besides jaw closing lowering the first formant, singers may relax breath support too soon on a voiced final consonant like [m], making the pitch flat.
